items.text: SEASON 10 · EPISODE 4 · DRAFT · CASE-053  Coldframe Sound, Studio A · week two · Maya, Esme, Corbin (the label’s product manager) and Pim · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  Esme can’t find the ballad. She says she’s behind herself; the label says she’s tired. Somebody says “session singer”, and the room goes quiet.  ⚑ RV-176: her album, her call. RV-180: her voice is shown with care, and stopping is hers to choose. RV-177: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: Latency You Can Feel
items.stakes: Esme can't sing the ballad in time, and the label is talking about a session singer.
items.reward: Her own voice back in her ears — and the ballad sung by her.

objectives.text: Decide how to fix her headphones
Decide how the label hears about it

items.rumor: Measure the path, not the person.

items.alt: The live room with the drum kit moved aside; Esme stands at the vocal microphone, headphones on, arms wrapped round herself; Maya by the door.

bubbles.text: It's like singing into a room next door. I'm always a hair behind.
Then let's find out how far away the room is.

items.caption: The ballad, take eleven.

lines.text: It's like singing into a room next door.
Then let's find out how far away the room is.

items.prompt: 14:15. Esme can't sing in time. Corbin says ‘session singer’. What first?
items.risk: An artist replaced on her own album for a studio fault.
timeout: Corbin makes a call to a session singer.

hints.text: What could you measure between her mouth and her ears?

options.label: Agree to try a session singer on the ballad
options.result: Esme hears about it from the corridor. She doesn't sing again today.
options.consequence: Treats a possible fault as a verdict on the artist — and it's not your call.
options.fail: Who sings on her album is the artist's decision, not a fix for a fault.

options.label: Measure what she hears: clap into her mic and record the headphone feed at the same moment
options.result: The headphone copy lands 27.3 ms after the clap.
options.consequence: Measure the path before anyone judges the person.

options.label: Tell her to sing a little ahead of the beat
options.result: She tries. The ballad sounds anxious.
options.consequence: Asks the performer to compensate for the studio.

options.label: Turn her voice down in her headphones
options.result: She pushes to hear herself; by take three her voice is tired.
options.consequence: Makes her work harder — and strains her voice (RV-180).

items.title: Twenty-seven milliseconds.
items.body: The clap and its copy in the headphones sit 27.3 ms apart. Maya reads every setting on the path: the buffer went from 128 to 512 samples on Tuesday — Pim, stopping the rough-mix plug-ins from crackling — which alone is 21.3 ms for the round trip. The converters add a millisecond. That leaves five.
items.label: Test: what did the buffer change cost her — and how far away does that put her?

items.sub: Mastery · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Esme and Maya beside a board. I'm behind myself. I hear me a hair late, like a room I'm not in. Corbin thinks I'm just tired. The buffer went to five hundred and twelve samples on Tuesday, and there's a limiter with lookahead on your vocal. Is that enough to hear?

bubbles.text: I'm behind myself. I hear me a hair late, like a room I'm not in. Corbin thinks I'm just tired.

items.label: **Sort it:** where does the delay come from?

items.alt: A timing sheet from 0 to 30 milliseconds: a bar made of the converter, a 10.7 ms input buffer, 5 ms of lookahead, a 10.7 ms output buffer and the converter again, ending at 27.3 ms; a dashed blue line at 2.9 ms marks one metre from a monitor wedge.
items.caption: Nine metres from her own voice.

items.title: Tue 18:12 · buffer 128 → 512
items.body: The recording program's settings history: ‘Tue 18:12 — buffer size 128 → 512 (P.)’. Pim's note beside it: ‘crackles in rough mix, fixed.’ Fixed for the mix; broken for the singer.

items.title: Playing along with yourself
items.body: Tape machines record on one head and play back on another a little further along the tape, so a musician overdubbing while listening to the playback head heard the band late — and played late. In the mid-1950s Ross Snyder, an engineer at an American tape-recorder maker, let the record head itself play back the tracks being played along to. Everything lined up; multitrack overdubbing, as studios came to know it, followed.

items.title: Early and late.
items.body: The last five milliseconds are a limiter with lookahead on her headphone feed — Corbin's request on Monday, ‘so she sounds finished’. And there's a second copy of her voice Maya can't turn off: the one Esme hears through her own head, instantly. Anything late in the headphones combs against it. A few milliseconds sounds hollow; twenty-seven sounds like singing next door.
items.label: Test: where does a small delay land in her own head — and whose call is the ballad?

items.alt: The control room; Corbin, arms folded, looks at the timing sheet on the screen; Maya beside it.

bubbles.text: I asked for the limiter. I wanted her to feel like a finished record.
It made her feel like a record playing in the next room.

items.prompt: I wasn't trying to replace her. I was trying to hit the date.

options.label: “I believe you. So give her the date back — tell her, in front of me, that the fault was ours.”
options.reply: …Fine. Yes. She should hear it from me.

options.label: “It sounded like replacing her.”
options.reply: Then I said it badly. It's a hard week.

options.label: “The date isn't my problem.”
options.reply: It's everyone's problem. That's the label.

items.prompt: 27.3 ms: 21.3 of buffers, 5 of lookahead, 1 of converters. What's the fix?
unknown: Whether she'll want to sing today
items.risk: A ballad sung against the clock and against her own ears.
timeout: She sings take twelve into the same delay.

hints.text: Does her voice need to go through the computer at all to reach her ears?

options.label: Drop the buffer to 64 samples
options.result: About 8.7 ms — and the mix plug-ins crackle again.
options.consequence: Trades her comfort for the mix, and still leaves the lookahead.

options.label: Direct monitoring through the personal cue mixer, before the computer; a zero-latency reverb on the cue mixer for comfort; no lookahead on her path; record her dry; leave the buffer where mixing needs it
options.result: About 1.5 ms from her mouth to her ears. The buffer stays at 512 for the mix.
options.consequence: Take the computer out of her ears instead of fighting it.

options.label: Buffer to 128 and remove the limiter
options.result: About 6.3 ms: better, and still hollow for a singer.
options.consequence: Closer — the computer's still in the loop.

options.label: Take her headphones off and play the band through the speakers
options.result: The band bleeds into her vocal mic.
options.consequence: Solves latency by ruining the recording.

items.label: **Fix it:** take the computer out of Esme's ears.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #95 · AVERY'S LENS  Measure what the performer hears  A performer's headphones are part of the instrument. Measure the delay from her mouth to her ears, keep the computer out of that path, and never let a fault be mistaken for the artist.  Twenty-seven milliseconds of a singer's own voice arriving late nearly got her replaced on her own album.

items.alt: The timing sheet after the fix: a short green bar — converter in, cue mixer, converter out — ending at 1.5 ms, well inside the 2.9 ms line for one metre from a wedge.
items.caption: Closer than a wedge.

items.title: ‘make her sound finished in the cans’
items.body: Corbin's email from Monday: ‘Can we put the mastering limiter on her headphone feed? She'll perform better if she sounds finished.’ Kindly meant. Five milliseconds.

items.prompt: The ballad's in, in two takes. Corbin still wants a session singer ‘as insurance’. How does the label hear what happened?
items.risk: An artist who believes the fault was her.

hints.text: Who needs to hear it — and from whom will they believe it?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S10E04). Option B needs Authority & access at LIMITED or better.

options.label: Stay out of it — it's between Esme and the label
options.result: Corbin's ‘insurance’ email goes to the label's head office that night.

options.label: Walk Esme and Corbin through the measurement together; say plainly that the fault was the studio's and is fixed; what happens next is Esme's call with her label
options.result: Corbin reads the sheet, then says it to Esme himself: ‘It was never you.’ The insurance idea dies in the room.
options.consequence: Evidence, said to the person it was about, by people the label trusts.

options.label: Email the measurement to Hollis and Corbin and let Hollis argue it
options.result: It takes three days. Esme sings the next song under a cloud.
options.consequence: The right facts — slow, and without the trust to land them today.

options.label: Record a guide vocal with a session singer ‘just in case’, without telling Esme
options.result: She finds the file on Friday.
options.consequence: A copy of her song made behind her back.
options.fail: Recording her song with someone else behind her back breaks her trust and isn't yours to do.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A performer’s headphones are part of her instrument. Measure mouth to ear (t = 2B ÷ fₛ + converters + plug-ins); keep lookahead out of the cue path; monitor direct through the cue mixer so the computer’s buffer can be what the mix needs; record dry. A singer also hears herself through her own head, so a few milliseconds sounds hollow. Never let a studio fault become a verdict on the artist.
REFLECTION (optional)  · When someone says “it feels wrong”, what could you measure before anyone decides it’s them?
